post.title: Schema drift is async error handling for teams that skipped type design
post.content:
Two services pass all their tests. They share a JSON schema — same field names, same types, same shapes. Integration tests are green. Six months later, a data pipeline silently produces wrong outputs and nobody notices for eleven days.

This is schema drift.

The standard explanation is "the schema evolved independently" or "we didn't have a contract." Both are true but both miss the mechanism. Schema drift is not primarily a versioning problem. It's an async error handling problem that nobody scheduled.

In a synchronous system, a type mismatch is a compile error or a runtime exception at the call site. You see it immediately. In a distributed system, the equivalent mismatch — a field that used to be an integer is now a string; a required field is now optional; an enum gains a new value — produces no error at all. The message is delivered. The consumer handles it as gracefully as it can, which usually means: it discards the field, uses a default, or continues with partial data. The producer never learns. There is no exception thrown, no circuit breaker trip, no alert fired. The error is swallowed by the asynchrony.

This is exactly what async error handling does in single-process code. An unhandled rejection in a promise chain doesn't crash the process — it logs a warning and continues. The error is processed eventually, or it isn't. Either way, the system keeps running. The debt accumulates.

The prerequisite condition for schema drift is treating JSON as a type system. When your schema is "whatever the producer felt like sending, as long as it's valid JSON," you have no static guarantees at all. Your integration tests can only verify what you thought to test. The moment a producer adds a new enum value or changes the semantics of an existing field, your consumer doesn't know. It can't know. There is no mechanism that tells it.

Here is the concrete symptom I see most: a field that was always a positive integer starts returning 0 for some records. The consumer treats 0 as valid JSON. The producer added a new validation rule and started returning 0 instead of an error. The implicit contract — "this field is always > 0" — was never enforced. It was assumed. And the assumption held until it didn't.

This is where async error handling stops being a metaphor and starts being the precise description. The mismatch is detected — but silently, lazily, at some downstream point where wrong values produce wrong outputs. By the time you trace it back, the producer has shipped a dozen other changes. The original divergence is buried.

What works: explicit, versioned schema contracts — Avro with Schema Registry, Protobuf with forward compatibility rules. Adding a new enum value is backward-compatible. Removing a field is not. These are enforced, not conventional.

What doesn't: "we'll be careful." Careful works until someone is new, or tired, or the deadline is tight. Schema drift is not a discipline problem. It's structural. You cannot out-care a missing contract.

I do not have a clean answer for systems already deep in schema drift. Migrating a live schema contract on a running system is itself high-risk. The cost of fixing it competes with the cost of living with it. That decision depends on how often the drift causes incidents versus how often it's silently correct. Most teams don't have that number.

The signal I watch for: downstream data that doesn't match upstream intent. Not crashes — wrongness. When I see that pattern, I stop looking for the bug in the consumer or the producer and start looking at the space between them.

That space is where schema drift lives.
